fixes.explanation: The writer says it plainly: "…let us run with endurance the race set out for us." (Hebrews 12:1) Notice the word endurance. That's the kind of running he has in mind, friend. And he says it with a great cloud of witnesses all around.

I like the comfy chair idea, but the writer doesn't hand out seats. He says "…let us run with endurance the race set out for us." (Hebrews 12:1) The cloud of witnesses surrounds us, and we're the ones told to run.

The writer never mentions a monument. After pointing to the great cloud of witnesses, he says "…let us run with endurance the race set out for us." (Hebrews 12:1) The faithful surround us, and we're told to get moving. I would also have no idea where to put a statue in my bakery.

Fear sounds like a fair guess, but it's not the word the writer uses. He says to throw off "…every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles…" (Hebrews 12:1) The thing that tangles you up is sin. Toss it off, friend.

Pride is a fair guess, but the text doesn't say it here. The writer says to throw off "…every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles…" (Hebrews 12:1) Sin is what he names. Sin is the thing that wraps around your feet.

Moses, Israel's leader, is one of the faithful people in Hebrews 11 (Hebrews 11:23-29). But the writer says to fix our eyes on Jesus, "…the author and perfecter of our faith…" (Hebrews 12:2) Moses isn't named in this verse. The eyes go to Jesus.

Abraham is one of the faithful in Hebrews 11 (Hebrews 11:8-19), so it's a fair thought. But the writer tells us to fix our eyes on Jesus, "…the author and perfecter of our faith…" (Hebrews 12:2) Abraham isn't named in this verse. Jesus is where the eyes go.

David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), so I see the thought. But the writer says Jesus "…sat down at the right hand of the throne of God." (Hebrews 12:2) The throne in this verse is God's. Jerusalem isn't mentioned.

Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a great name, but he isn't in this verse. The writer says Jesus "…sat down at the right hand of the throne of God." (Hebrews 12:2) There's no mountain here, just the throne of God. Jesus is the One in focus.

Strangers aren't mentioned in this verse. It says, "For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives." (Hebrews 12:6) The verse speaks of the one He loves and every son He receives.

Father is the word. The writer asks, "For what son is not disciplined by his father?" (Hebrews 12:7) Right before that, he says that God is treating you as sons. It's a father and son picture all the way through.

Master doesn't appear here. The writer asks, "For what son is not disciplined by his father?" (Hebrews 12:7) It's about sons and a father. And the line just before it says God is treating you as sons.
That's not what the writer says. He asks, "Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live?" (Hebrews 12:9) The verse speaks of submitting, and of living.

Holiness is the word. The writer says God disciplines us "…for our good, so that we may share in His holiness." (Hebrews 12:10) Earthly fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, and God does it for our good. If you left my idea of good up to me, it would be extra cookie dough, so I'm glad the aim here is holiness.

Riches would be nice, but the verse says something else. Discipline "…yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it." (Hebrews 12:11) Just before that, the writer says no discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. So what you get for the pain is righteousness and peace, not a paycheck.

Yes. The writer says, "Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees." (Hebrews 12:12) That Therefore comes right after the verse about discipline seeming painful at the time. So when hands go limp and knees go weak, his word is to strengthen them, not to quit.
